text: Ada came home to find her flatmate had eaten the dinner she had spent two hours making for her mother's visit, and left the dirty pot in the sink. Her mother was arriving in thirty minutes. Ada stood in the kitchen with her coat still on, her jaw clenched so hard her teeth ached. Heat surged up her neck. She picked up the pot and slammed it down in the sink so hard it rang. When her flatmate wandered in and said, oh, was that yours, Ada's hands balled into fists and she had to walk out of the room before she threw the pot at the wall.

Gus's landlord let himself into the flat without warning while Gus was cooking, and began criticizing the grease on the stove, the dishes, the smell. He had raised the rent twice this year and fixed nothing. Gus gripped the wooden spoon until his knuckles went white. His pulse was thumping in his temples. The landlord opened the fridge and peered inside. That was it. Gus turned off the flame, turned around, and told him in a low, shaking voice to get out of his home, now, and his whole body was trembling with the effort of not shouting.

For the third time that week the bus drove straight past Oren's stop without slowing, the driver looking right at him. Oren had been waiting in the rain for twenty minutes. He would be late again, and his supervisor had warned him. He stood in the road shouting after the bus, his face hot, his hands shaking. A woman at the shelter shook her head in sympathy. Oren kicked the shelter wall so hard his foot throbbed. His chest was heaving. He took out his phone and began typing a complaint, jabbing at the screen with his thumb.

A driver cut across three lanes and swerved in front of Pia, forcing her to brake so hard her coffee flew across the dashboard. Then he slowed down and made a rude gesture out of his window. Pia's face burned. She gripped the wheel, her teeth clenched, the blood pounding in her ears. She leaned on the horn and kept leaning on it. Coffee was dripping onto her new trousers. At the next red light she pulled up beside him, and he laughed at her through the glass, and she felt something hot and violent rise up in her chest.

Kai's brother called to say he had sold their late father's watch, the one their father had promised to Kai, to pay off a gambling debt. He said it casually, as if it were nothing. Kai felt the heat rise from his stomach into his face. He stood up. His voice, when it came, was loud and shaking. His brother said he was overreacting. Kai slammed his palm on the table so hard the mugs jumped. He hung up and paced the room, breathing hard, his fists opening and closing, his whole body humming like a struck wire.

Ines's sister called to announce that she had told the whole family Ines's private news, the pregnancy Ines had asked her to keep secret for another month. She said she could not help it. Ines stood in the hallway with the phone pressed to her ear, her heart pounding, her face hot. Her mother would already be telling the neighbors. The one thing she had asked. Her jaw was so tight it hurt. She said her sister's name once, very quietly, and then hung up, and threw the phone onto the sofa, and stood there shaking.

In the meeting Esme's manager presented her project, the one she had worked on every weekend for two months, as his own. He did not mention her once. The director praised him warmly. Esme sat at the end of the table with her pen gripped so hard it bent. Her face was burning and her heart was hammering against her ribs. She could feel her pulse in her neck. When the manager glanced at her and smiled, she had to press her feet hard into the floor to stop herself from standing up and shouting the truth across the room.

Bram's boss announced that the overtime they had all worked through the summer would not be paid after all, because of the budget. He said it with a shrug and then left early for his holiday. Bram stood by the machines with his fists clenched, the heat rising up his neck. Nineteen weekends. He thought of his daughter's school trip he had promised to pay for. His breathing was fast and heavy. He picked up a wrench and slammed it down on the workbench, and the sound rang across the whole floor, and nobody said anything.

Lale came out in the morning to find that someone had driven a motorbike across her vegetable garden in the night, churning the beds into mud and snapping every bean pole. The tire tracks led straight to the neighbor's gate. His son had been warned twice. Lale's hands started to shake. Heat flooded her face. She marched across the lawn in her dressing gown, her jaw set, and hammered on the neighbor's door with her fist, again and again, until the frame rattled, her breath coming hard and fast, ready to say every word she had held back all year.

The council workers had cut down the old pear tree in Teo's front garden by mistake, reading the wrong address on the job sheet. It had been planted by his grandfather. They stood there with their chainsaw, shrugging, saying it was not their problem. Teo felt the blood pound in his temples. His hands clenched into fists at his sides. He told them exactly what he thought of them in a voice that carried down the whole street. His face was hot and his chest tight. When they drove off, laughing, he threw a clod of earth after their van.

Rafa had waited four hours in the clinic with his feverish daughter when the receptionist told him their appointment had been given away because he had not confirmed it by text. He had confirmed it. He showed her the message. She shrugged and said the system was the system. Rafa's jaw clenched. Heat rose through his chest and into his face. His daughter was shivering against his side. He leaned over the counter and, in a voice that made the whole waiting room go quiet, demanded to see a doctor, now, his hand shaking on the desk.

The doctor would not look up from his screen while Vera explained her symptoms for the third time. He cut her off mid-sentence, told her it was stress, and began typing a prescription for sleeping pills. Vera had been ill for eight months. Something hot and hard rose in her chest. Her hands gripped the arms of the chair. She said, loudly, that she was not finished. He sighed. Vera's face was burning. She stood, snatched the prescription out of the printer, tore it in half, and dropped the pieces on his keyboard.

The letter from the insurance company said Femi's claim for the flood damage had been rejected, on a technicality buried on page thirty of the policy. He had paid them every month for eleven years. Femi read it twice, standing in his ruined kitchen with the carpet still stinking. His face went hot. He crushed the letter in his fist. His heart was hammering, and he could hear himself breathing through his nose. He picked up the phone and dialed the number with stabbing fingers, and when the hold music began he slammed his hand against the wall.

Noor opened the parcel to find that the handmade quilt she had ordered for her mother's birthday had been swapped for a cheap printed blanket, and the seller had stopped answering messages. She had paid three hundred for it. Noor's jaw tightened and a hot pressure rose behind her eyes. She threw the blanket across the room. Her hands were shaking as she typed a review, deleting the words that were too savage, then typing them back. Her heart was pounding. She walked around the flat twice, fists clenched, before she could sit still.

Zola found her neighbor's boy throwing stones at her cat, who had crawled under the hedge with a bleeding ear. The boy laughed when he saw her. Zola's vision narrowed. The blood roared in her ears. She crossed the lawn in three strides and caught his wrist, and the stones dropped to the ground. Her voice came out low and hard, shaking with force. When his mother appeared and told her to take her hands off her son, Zola turned on her too, her face burning, and told her exactly what her son had been doing.

Jun's neighbor had reported his dog to the council for barking, even though the dog had been at the vet all week. Now there was an official warning letter pinned to Jun's door, threatening a fine. Jun stood on the landing reading it, the heat climbing up his neck, his jaw clenched. That neighbor had been making trouble for months. Jun ripped the letter off the door and knocked on the neighbor's, and when it opened he held the paper up and began talking, his voice rising with every word, his hand trembling around the page.

The movers arrived five hours late, dropped Hana's grandmother's mirror on the stairs, and then demanded an extra hundred in cash before they would unload the rest of her furniture. The truck held everything she owned. Hana stood on the pavement, her whole body tense, her face hot, fists clenched at her sides. The man chewed gum and waited. She told him she would call the police. He shrugged and started to close the truck doors. Hana stepped in front of him, shaking, and slapped her hand flat against the metal, her voice cracking as she shouted.

When Zeb moved out, his landlord kept the whole deposit, claiming damage to a carpet that had been threadbare when Zeb moved in. Zeb had photographs. The landlord would not look at them. He said take it to court if you like, and smirked. Zeb's hands shook. The heat rose to his face and his heart thudded hard and fast. He stood in the empty flat and felt his fists clench so hard his nails dug into his palms. On the way out he slammed the door so hard a picture fell off the wall inside.

A car door swung open right in front of Wren as she cycled past, and she hit it and went over the handlebars onto the road. The driver got out and shouted at her for scratching his paint. Wren lay on the tarmac with her elbow bleeding and her wheel bent, and a hot surge rose from her stomach into her throat. She got up, shaking, and walked toward him. Her voice came out much louder than she meant it to. When he told her cyclists should not be on the road, she smacked her palm down on his car roof.

Amir came out of the library to find someone had stolen the saddle and both wheels from his bicycle, leaving the frame chained to the rack like a skeleton. It was the second time this month. The security camera above the rack, he had been told last time, was fake. He stood staring at the stripped frame, his face growing hot, his jaw tight. He kicked the rack so hard it clanged. His heart was pounding. He went back into the library and demanded to see the manager, his voice ringing off the quiet walls.

At the market a man shoved in front of Vera in the queue, and when she said something he told her to shut up, old woman. The seller served him anyway. Vera felt heat flood her face and a trembling start in her hands. She had been standing there twenty minutes on her bad hip. She stepped forward and put her hand on the counter between them. Her voice, when it came, was sharp and loud enough to turn heads across the market. Her heart was hammering, but she did not step back, and she did not lower her voice.

The stall holder sold Eli a bag of fruit that turned out to be rotten underneath, the good ones carefully layered on top. When Eli brought it back, the man denied ever seeing him and laughed with the stall next door. Eli's jaw clenched until his teeth hurt. He could feel his pulse in his temples. He tipped the bag out onto the counter, the rotten plums splitting and oozing, and his voice rose until people stopped to look. His hands were shaking and his face was burning hot, and he let them all stare.

On a rainy afternoon Cleo found that her teenage son had taken her car without asking, driven it to a party, and brought it back with a crumpled wing and an empty tank. He was asleep upstairs. Cleo stood in the rain looking at the dent, her fists clenched, the water running down her face. Her heart was pounding and her whole body felt hot despite the cold. She went inside, climbed the stairs two at a time, and threw open his door so hard it banged against the wall, and said his name in a voice that shook the room.

Rain kept Sami indoors, and he spent the afternoon on hold with the phone company, who had cut off his internet by mistake. Every time he got through to a person, the line dropped. On the fifth call a man told him there was no record of his account. Sami's jaw was clenched so hard his face ached. Heat pulsed in his temples. He stood up, too fast, knocking over his chair. He was shouting now, he noticed, and did not stop, his free hand slamming the table in time with his words.

Nell's friend came to visit and spent the whole evening mocking Nell's new job, her flat, her boyfriend, all with a little smile, as if it were a joke. Nell had cooked for her. By the fourth remark, Nell's face was hot and her jaw was tight. Her hands gripped her fork. When her friend laughed at the painting Nell had made, something snapped. Nell put down her glass so hard the wine sloshed out, and said, her voice shaking with force, that it was time for her to leave.

Ivo's old friend came to stay for a weekend, and Ivo came home from work to find the friend had thrown a party in his flat, with twenty strangers, music blaring, a broken lamp, and cigarette burns on the sofa. The friend waved at him from the kitchen, beer in hand. Ivo's face went hot. Something hard and burning rose from his chest. He crossed the room, pulled the plug on the speaker, and in the sudden silence told everyone to get out, his voice loud and shaking, his fists clenched.

The garage returned Rhea's old car with a bill three times the quote and the same rattle it had gone in with. The mechanic said they had found other problems. Nobody had called her. Rhea stood at the counter, her face burning, her jaw tight. The mechanic kept eating his sandwich. Her heart was pounding. She slapped the bill down on the counter and demanded to see every part they had replaced, her voice rising until the other customers turned around, and her hand was shaking where it lay on the paper.

Someone had keyed a long jagged line down the side of Tavi's old car, from the headlight to the tail, and written a slur in the dust on the windscreen. It was the third time since he moved to this street. Tavi stood by the car, his whole body rigid, the blood pounding in his ears, his hands curled into fists. He looked up at the windows of the houses opposite. A curtain twitched. He walked straight across the road and banged on the door, over and over, his breath coming hard.

At pickup Bea's son came out with a torn shirt and a scraped cheek, and told her the same boy had pushed him again, and the teacher had done nothing, again. Bea felt the heat rush into her face. Her jaw clenched. She marched into the school, holding her son's hand, straight past the receptionist and into the head teacher's office without knocking. Her voice, when she spoke, was low and shaking. Her heart was pounding. She put both hands flat on the desk and said she was not leaving until something was done.

A driver double-parked across the school crossing where the children came out, and when Quin asked him to move he rolled up his window and turned his music up. A little girl had to step out into the road to get around the car. Quin's face went hot and his pulse hammered. He banged on the driver's window with his fist. The man ignored him. Quin stood in front of the car's bonnet, arms spread, his whole body trembling, shouting that he would not move until the car did.

On the beach a group of young men played loud music, threw their empty cans into the sea, and laughed when Yara asked them to stop. One of them threw a can at her feet. Yara felt the blood rush to her face and her fists clench. The heat in her chest was so strong she could hardly breathe. She picked up the can, walked straight up to the one who had thrown it, and dropped it in his lap. Her voice came out loud and hard, and she did not give a thought to who was watching.

At the lake a speedboat roared through the roped-off swimming area, missing Zeb's children by a few feet and swamping them with its wake. The driver laughed and circled back. Zeb stood waist-deep in the water, holding his coughing daughter, his heart hammering, heat flooding his face. His fists clenched. He waded toward the jetty as the boat came in to dock, and when the driver stepped off, still grinning, Zeb grabbed the rope and would not let him tie up, shouting into his face until the man stopped grinning.
